text: Scam knowledge: Tech-support scammers claim to be Microsoft, Apple, Norton or Geek Squad, say the computer has a virus, and ask the person to install remote-control software such as AnyDesk, TeamViewer or UltraViewer. Microsoft never calls people about viruses.
Scam knowledge: A caller who asks for payment in gift cards (Google Play, Apple, Steam, Amazon) is always a scam. No company, bank, court or government agency accepts gift cards.
Scam knowledge: Wire transfers, Zelle, Western Union, crypto and Bitcoin ATMs cannot be reversed. Scammers insist on them because the money cannot be recovered.

Scam knowledge: The refund scam says you were overcharged by Amazon, Norton or Geek Squad and must call a number to get a refund. The caller then pretends to refund too much and asks you to send the difference back with gift cards.

Scam knowledge: The grandparent scam is a call or text saying 'it's me, I crashed the car, I'm in jail, I need bail money, don't tell anyone'. The caller pretends to be a grandchild or child from a different number and asks for secrecy and urgency.
Scam knowledge: Asking the person to keep it secret from the rest of the family is the strongest single sign of a scam. Real relatives and real companies never ask for secrecy.

Scam knowledge: Scammers create urgency: 'within 24 hours', 'right now', 'your account will be closed', 'the police are on their way'. Urgency is designed to stop the person from checking with family.

Scam knowledge: Fake bank texts say the account is locked or blocked and give a link to 'verify'. The link goes to a copy of the bank's login page on a domain the bank does not own, created days earlier, which collects the password and card number.
Scam knowledge: Keystone Bank never sends links by text. The domain keystone-verifica.top is a known fake Keystone Bank login page created to steal passwords and card numbers.
Scam knowledge: Short links such as bit.ly, tinyurl and t.ly hide the real destination. Banks, courier companies and government agencies do not use short links in texts.
Scam knowledge: The package delivery scam says a USPS, FedEx or UPS parcel could not be delivered and asks for a small fee of $1 to $3 through a link. The purpose is the card number, not the fee.
Scam knowledge: The Netflix or streaming billing scam says the payment failed and asks for updated card details on a look-alike domain such as netflx-billing.online.

Scam knowledge: The Social Security or Medicare scam says the person's number has been suspended or used in a crime and asks them to confirm the number or move money to a 'safe account'. The SSA never suspends numbers and never calls about them.
Scam knowledge: The IRS scam threatens arrest for unpaid taxes and demands payment by gift card or wire. The IRS contacts people by mail first and never demands gift cards.
Scam knowledge: The 'safe account' scam says the bank account is compromised and the money must be moved to a new account the caller provides. Banks never ask customers to move money to protect it.
Scam knowledge: A one-time passcode or OTP must never be read to anyone on the phone. Scammers ask for the code to log in as the person. Banks never ask for the code they just sent.
Scam knowledge: Callers who give a different number to call back, instead of the number printed on the card or bill, are steering the person to a scam call centre.
Scam knowledge: A real company or agency can be checked by hanging up and calling the number on the card, the bill or the official website. A scam cannot survive that call.

Scam knowledge: Remote-control software gives the caller full control of the computer, including online banking. Once installed, the caller can hide the screen and move money while the person watches a fake 'scan'.
Scam knowledge: Scam pop-ups on the computer say 'do not turn off your PC' and show a phone number. Turning the computer off is safe; the pop-up is a web page, not a system message.
Scam knowledge: Romance and friendship scams build trust over weeks before asking for money for a medical emergency, customs fees or a plane ticket. The request for money is the scam.
Scam knowledge: Lottery and prize scams say the person has won but must pay a fee or tax first. Real prizes never require payment to collect.
Scam knowledge: Voice cloning lets scammers imitate a relative's voice on a call. The way to check is to call the relative back on the number the family saved, not the number that called.
Scam knowledge: Scammers spoof caller ID so the call appears to come from the bank or the police. Caller ID proves nothing; only calling back on the saved number does.

Scam knowledge: In Telugu-speaking families the bail scam often says 'అమ్మా నేను, కారు యాక్సిడెంట్ అయింది, పోలీస్ స్టేషన్‌లో ఉన్నాను, ఎవరికీ చెప్పొద్దు' (Amma it's me, car accident, at the police station, don't tell anyone). The secrecy line is the sign.
Scam knowledge: In Telugu the urgency words are వెంటనే (immediately), అర్జెంట్ (urgent), ఇప్పుడే (right now) and 24 గంటల్లో (within 24 hours). Gift cards are గిఫ్ట్ కార్డులు and a wire is వైర్.
Scam knowledge: In Spanish the bail scam says 'Mamá, choqué el carro, estoy detenido, necesito dinero para la fianza, no le digas a nadie'. 'No le digas a nadie' is the secrecy line.
Scam knowledge: In Spanish, fake bank texts say 'Su cuenta está bloqueada. Verifique en 24 horas' with a link. Real banks in Spanish-speaking markets also do not send verification links by text.

Scam knowledge: Scammers target older adults because they are more likely to answer unknown calls, more trusting of authority, and less likely to tell their children out of embarrassment. Telling family is the defence.
Scam knowledge: After one successful scam, the same person is often targeted again within weeks, sometimes by a 'recovery' scam that promises to get the money back for a fee.
Scam knowledge: A bank, a court or the police will never ask a person to buy gift cards, read the numbers from the back, or deposit cash in a Bitcoin ATM.
Scam knowledge: Cash courier scams send someone to the person's home to collect cash or gold 'for the police' or 'for bail'. No agency collects cash at the door.
Scam knowledge: QR codes in unexpected texts or on parking meters can lead to payment pages controlled by scammers. Only scan QR codes from a trusted source.
Scam knowledge: A domain registered only days ago that imitates a well-known brand is almost always a phishing page. Real bank domains are years old.
Scam knowledge: A message that mixes a trusted brand name with an address on .top, .xyz, .online, .site or .click is a phishing message. Brands use their own domain.
Scam knowledge: If a caller says 'do not hang up' or 'stay on the line while you go to the store', they are controlling the person to stop them from thinking or calling family.
Scam knowledge: The safest answer to any request for money or codes is: 'I will send this to Guardian first, and my family will call you back on the number we have.'
Scam knowledge: Guardian never asks anyone for codes, passwords, card numbers or payments, and never approves money. Only a family member's press-and-hold can approve a payment.
